name: Multani mitti (fuller's earth)

lead: Fuller's earth is a family of absorbent clays, typically palygorskite or bentonite, historically used to remove grease from wool.[1] Multani mitti, meaning clay of Multan, is its best-known cosmetic form and is widely used in the Indian subcontinent in face packs.[1]

People use it to soak up facial oil and dirt. The Wikipedia article notes that on pigmentation such as melasma it is sometimes called whitening clay.[1] A safety review by the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel found naturally sourced clays safe as used in cosmetics, with insufficient data for products that may be inhaled.[2]

paras: Traditionally the powder is mixed with water or other liquids into a paste, applied as a face pack and rinsed off after drying. Some people mix it with ingredients such as rosewater.

The panel flagged insufficient data for incidental inhalation, and bentonite reviews identify respirable dust as the main exposure concern, as some clays can contain crystalline silica.[2][3] Drying of skin is commonly noted.

chain: Clay absorbs sebum and surface dirt
Less shine and a fresher-looking complexion
angle.text: Face packs of Multani mitti are used to absorb excess oil and impurities, giving a matte finish. Traditional users also use it for evening out tone, a claim described as common in the Indian subcontinent.

lead: Fuller's earth is a family of absorbent clays, commonly palygorskite (attapulgite) or bentonite, used for centuries to clean wool and today as absorbents, filters, bleaching agents and cosmetic ingredients. Multani mitti, meaning clay of Multan after the city in present-day Pakistan, is its best-known cosmetic form and is widely used in face packs across the Indian subcontinent.[1]

The appearance use is oil control and a cleaner, matte complexion. The clay's ability to soak up oil and dirt, the property that once cleaned lanolin from wool, is applied to oily or congested skin as a mask, and Wikipedia notes it is sometimes called whitening clay when used on facial pigmentation such as melasma.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as drawing out impurities and controlling excess oil in face packs, especially for acne-prone skin.[2]

Research on appearance outcomes is absent, but safety reviews exist. In a 2026 amended assessment the Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel concluded naturally sourced clays are safe as used in cosmetics, with insufficient data for products that may be inhaled.[3] A review of bentonite toxicology identified inhalation of respirable dust by occupationally exposed workers as the principal concern.[4]

paras: The name comes from fullers, textile workers who used the clay to clean and thicken wool by absorbing lanolin and oils. Commercial fuller's earth mostly contains palygorskite or bentonite; the wider family is hydrous aluminium silicates, including montmorillonite, kaolinite and attapulgite, with small amounts of calcite, dolomite and quartz.[1] In some places the term refers to calcium bentonite, an altered volcanic ash.[1] Grokipedia adds that southeastern US deposits are mainly attapulgite and European ones montmorillonite, and that the powder is pale and fine-grained with high surface area.[2]
In South Asia the material is called multani mitti, mud from Multan, a city historically associated with high-quality deposits and trade in the clay.[1][2]

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: Multani mitti is widely used in face packs in the Indian subcontinent, applied as a paste of the powder and a liquid and rinsed off after drying.[1] The target is oily, shiny or congested skin: as the clay dries it absorbs sebum and surface dirt, leaving a matte finish and, users say, a clearer, fresher-looking complexion.[2] The practice is described as traditional, with Grokipedia linking it to skin-care rituals dating to ancient times and to a 2020s resurgence of interest in natural and Ayurvedic ingredients.[2]

The same absorbency explains why the clay appears in beauty products as an absorbent and bulking agent, a role the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel lists for clay ingredients in cosmetics.[3] Wikipedia notes its use as a whitening clay on pigmentation such as melasma.[1]

Wikipedia reports that cuneiform texts from Mesopotamia mention a similar white earth and that Pliny the Elder described several types; fulling mills appeared in Persia and were widespread in the medieval world.[1] The clay appears in Arthur Conan Doyle's 1892 Sherlock Holmes story The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb.[1] Fuller's earth was first discovered in the United States near Quincy, Florida, in 1893; in 2005 the US produced almost 70 percent of the world's supply, ahead of Japan and Mexico.[1] In the UK the Combe Hay mine near Bath operated until 1979.[1]

Modern uses are mostly industrial: absorbents for oil, grease and animal waste, cat litter since the late 1940s, carriers for pesticides and fertilizers, filler in paint and pharmaceuticals, and decolorizer. It is also used in film makeup and dust effects, including the tornado in The Wizard of Oz (1939), and in skin decontamination after chemical exposure.[1]

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel assessed eight naturally sourced clay ingredients, all reported to function in cosmetics as absorbents and bulking agents, and found them safe as used, with data insufficient for products that may be inhaled.[3] Grokipedia states that the panel had assessed naturally sourced clays including fuller's earth as safe in 2023.[2]

A 2016 review in Inhalation Toxicology concluded that the main exposure pathway of concern for bentonite is inhalation of respirable dust by occupationally exposed cohorts, and that bentonite itself is probably not more toxic than other particulates not otherwise regulated.[4] A case-report literature describes pneumoconiosis from fuller's earth (montmorillonite) in workers.[5] Grokipedia says skin contact is generally non-toxic but repeated use may cause drying or mild irritation, and rare allergic reactions are reported.[2]
Wikipedia also notes that fuller's earth has been used in managing paraquat poisoning, a medical context unrelated to cosmetics.[1]

A 2018 Scientific Reports study described using fuller's earth and henna as cosmetic bases in a liposome system for transdermal folic acid delivery.[6] Studies of skin decontamination have compared fuller's earth formulations against chemical agents and a synthetic opioid in vitro.[7][8] These concern delivery and decontamination rather than facial appearance.
No studies found. Safety and toxicology reviews of clays exist, covering cosmetic use and inhalation exposure.[3][4]
